title: How Did Humans Invent Money?
notes: Series format: second-person narration, Byte as 'you' in visuals.

segments.text: Imagine you walk into a burger joint. You're starving.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) walking through the door of a cosy retro burger diner, hungry face, hand on his stomach, warm lights

segments.text: You order the biggest burger on the menu. Double patty. Extra cheese.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) sitting at the diner counter, a giant double cheeseburger on a plate in front of him, excited sparkly eyes
E: same scene and camera, Byte licks his lips and rubs his hands together

segments.text: You tap your card. Beep. Declined.
shots: S: close-up of a card reader on a diner counter showing a big red X, a bank card touching it, no people
B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) at the diner counter frozen in shock, eyes wide, sweat drop on his head

segments.text: You check your pockets. No cash. No coins. Nothing.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) pulling his empty hoodie pockets inside out, a single moth flying out, diner background

segments.text: The cook leans over the counter, looks at your hoodie, and says: I'll take that instead.
shots: S: a stickman cook with dot eyes and a small mouth in a white chef hat and apron leaning over a diner counter, pointing and grinning cheekily
B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) hugging his teal hoodie protectively, horrified face, diner counter

segments.text: Would you do it? Would you trade the hoodie off your back for a burger?
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) looking straight at the viewer with a thinking face, holding his hoodie in one hand and pointing at the burger with the other, diner

segments.text: Because for most of human history, that's not a joke. There were no coins. No cards. No apps.
shots: S: a stickman farmer with dot eyes and a small mouth in a straw hat in an ancient dusty village, shrugging with empty hands, mud huts behind

segments.text: So how did we go from trading hoodies and goats... to paying with invisible numbers on a screen?
shots: S: a goat standing in a dusty ancient field next to a sack of wheat, no people
S: close-up of a glowing smartphone screen showing a payment tick and glowing digits floating out of it, dark background, no people

segments.text: And why does a piece of paper with a number on it buy you a burger at all?
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) holding a green banknote up to the light, squinting at it suspiciously, plain warm background

segments.text: Stick around, because the answer is weirder than you think.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) leaning toward the viewer with a mischievous grin, finger raised, plain warm background

segments.text: It involves giant stones at the bottom of the ocean, a king so rich he became a saying, and pizzas that cost hundreds of millions of dollars.
shots: S: a giant round stone disc with a hole in the middle resting on the sandy sea floor, fish swimming past, sunbeams, no people
S: a stickman king with dot eyes and a small mouth with a golden crown sitting on a mountain of gold coins, laughing
S: two pizza boxes on a table with golden coins spilling out of them, glowing, no people

segments.text: Let's go back. Way back.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) being sucked into a swirling time portal full of flying coins and banknotes, comedic panic

segments.text: Here's the story you probably learned at school.
shots: S: a stickman teacher with dot eyes and a small mouth in a brown cardigan standing at a chalkboard, pointing at it with a stick, classroom

segments.text: Before money, people bartered. You have a goat. I have wheat. We swap. Easy.
shots: S: two stickmen with dot eyes and a small mouth in an ancient village, one in a straw hat holding a goat on a rope, the other in a red tunic holding a sack of wheat
E: same scene and camera, the two stickmen shake hands, both smiling

segments.text: Except it isn't easy at all.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) wagging his finger at the viewer with a knowing smirk, plain warm background

segments.text: What if you have a goat, but I don't want a goat? I want shoes.
shots: S: close-up of a stickman with dot eyes and a small mouth in a red tunic crossing his arms and shaking his head at a goat, a thought bubble with a pair of shoes above him, village

segments.text: Now you have to find someone who has shoes, and also wants a goat.
shots: S: a stickman with dot eyes and a small mouth in a straw hat dragging a stubborn goat through a busy ancient market, looking around, a few tiny distant stalls
E: same scene, the stickman looks exhausted and the goat chews his sleeve

segments.text: Economists even have a name for this headache. The double coincidence of wants.
shots: S: a stickman professor with dot eyes and a small mouth in round glasses and a tweed jacket holding a pointer next to a whiteboard with two overlapping circles, lecture hall

segments.text: And here's the twist your textbook skipped.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) slamming a big school textbook shut, dramatic face, plain warm background

segments.text: When anthropologists went looking for a society that actually ran on barter like this, they couldn't find one.
shots: S: a stickman explorer with dot eyes and a small mouth in a khaki pith helmet looking through binoculars on a jungle hill, a small village far below
E: same scene, the explorer lowers the binoculars and shrugs, confused

segments.text: Not one.
shots: S: close-up of the stickman explorer with dot eyes and a small mouth in a pith helmet crossing out the word barter in his notebook with a big pencil stroke

segments.text: So what did people really do? Something much simpler.
shots: S: a peaceful small ancient village of round huts at golden hour, smoke rising from chimneys, no people visible

segments.text: Imagine you live in a small village. Your neighbour needs bread. You give her some.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) in a simple tunic handing a basket of bread to a stickman woman neighbour with dot eyes and a small mouth with a red headscarf, village street

segments.text: She doesn't pay you. She owes you. And everybody in the village remembers.
shots: S: the stickman woman with dot eyes and a small mouth with a red headscarf holding the bread basket and giving a grateful thumbs up, village street
S: close-up of a wooden post with neat tally marks carved into it, village background, no people

segments.text: Next month, when you need help fixing your roof, guess who shows up.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) on a ladder fixing a thatched roof, the stickman woman with dot eyes and a small mouth with a red headscarf passing him straw from below, both smiling

segments.text: That's not barter. That's credit. In other words, debt came before coins.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) looking at the viewer with a raised eyebrow, a big glowing IOU note floating beside him, plain warm background

segments.text: But memory only works in a small village. What happens when your village grows into a city?
shots: S: an ancient Mesopotamian city of mud-brick houses with a tall stepped ziggurat temple, river and palm trees, a few tiny distant figures

segments.text: About five thousand years ago, in Mesopotamia, in what's now Iraq, cities had exactly that problem.
shots: S: aerial view of an ancient walled mud-brick city beside a wide river, fields of barley around it, golden light, no close-up people

segments.text: So temple officials started writing debts down. On clay tablets.
shots: S: a stickman scribe with dot eyes and a small mouth in a white wrap and headband pressing marks into a clay tablet with a reed stick, temple interior, oil lamp
E: same scene and camera, the scribe proudly holds up the finished tablet

segments.text: And here's something wild. Some of the oldest writing on Earth isn't poetry, or prayers. It's receipts.
shots: S: close-up of an ancient clay tablet covered in neat wedge-shaped marks on a wooden table, warm lamp light, no people
B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) holding a long paper shop receipt next to a clay tablet, grinning at the viewer, plain warm background

segments.text: Debts were counted in barley, and in silver, measured in a unit called the shekel.
shots: S: a stickman merchant with dot eyes and a small mouth in a striped robe weighing small pieces of silver on a balance scale next to sacks of barley, market stall

segments.text: But a shekel wasn't a coin. It was a weight. About eight grams of silver.
shots: S: close-up of a bronze balance scale with a small pile of silver on one side and a stone weight on the other, plain warm background, no people

segments.text: There was just one problem with all this debt. It kept piling up.
shots: S: a huge teetering stack of clay tablets piled up to the ceiling of a mud-brick storeroom, dramatic light, no people

segments.text: Farmers who had a bad harvest fell behind. Some lost their land. Some even had to work off their debts as servants.
shots: S: a sad stickman farmer with dot eyes and a small mouth in a straw hat standing in a dry cracked barley field with wilted crops, hot sun
E: same scene, the farmer drops to his knees and holds his head in his hands

segments.text: So every so often, a new king would do something amazing. He'd cancel the debts. All of them. A clean slate.
shots: S: a stickman king with dot eyes and a small mouth in a tall Mesopotamian crown standing on temple steps, raising both arms in a grand announcement
S: clay tablets shattering into pieces on a stone floor, dust flying, dramatic, no people

segments.text: The Sumerians had a word for it. Amargi. It literally means 'return to mother', because people freed from debt could go home to their families.
shots: S: a stickman farmer with dot eyes and a small mouth in a straw hat running happily into the open arms of a stickman mother with dot eyes and a small mouth in a long blue dress outside a mud-brick house, sunset

segments.text: Some historians call it one of the earliest written words we have for freedom.
shots: S: a single clay tablet glowing softly on a stone pedestal in a dark museum, spotlight, no people

segments.text: Meanwhile, in other parts of the world, people found other things to count with.
shots: S: a wide tropical coastline with turquoise water, wooden boats on the sand and palm trees, no people

segments.text: Like shells.
shots: S: close-up of a pile of shiny white cowrie shells spilling out of a woven basket on sand, warm light, no people

segments.text: Cowrie shells were small, shiny, tough, and almost impossible to fake.
shots: S: a stickman trader with dot eyes and a small mouth in a colourful wrap holding a single cowrie shell up to his eye and inspecting it, beach market

segments.text: For centuries, they were used as money across Asia, Africa and the Indian Ocean.
shots: S: two stickmen with dot eyes and a small mouth at a harbour market, one in a blue wrap handing a string of cowrie shells to the other in an orange wrap who holds a basket of fish
S: an old sailing ship with patched sails crossing a calm ocean at sunset, no people

segments.text: In fact, in Chinese writing, the old symbol for a shell became part of the words for money, wealth and buying.
shots: S: a stickman scholar with dot eyes and a small mouth in a dark blue robe and black cap painting a large simple shell-shaped symbol on a paper scroll with a brush, Chinese study room

segments.text: But if you think shells are strange, wait until you see the money on the island of Yap.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) raising his eyebrows with a 'wait for it' face, holding a cowrie shell, plain warm background

segments.text: Yap is a tiny island in the Pacific Ocean. And its money was... huge.
shots: S: aerial view of a small green tropical island surrounded by coral reef and deep blue ocean, no people

segments.text: Giant stone discs called rai. The biggest are about three and a half metres wide, and weigh around four tonnes.
shots: S: a giant round stone disc with a hole in the middle standing upright in a tropical village, a small stickman with dot eyes and a small mouth in a grass skirt standing beside it for scale, palm trees

segments.text: That's heavier than a car.
shots: S: a giant stone disc sitting on one side of a huge balance scale outweighing a small red car on the other side, plain warm background, no people

segments.text: The stones were carved on another island, hundreds of kilometres away, and brought home across the open ocean by canoe and raft.
shots: S: a stickman with dot eyes and a small mouth in a grass skirt chiselling a big round stone disc in a rocky quarry
S: a huge stone disc on a bamboo raft towed by an outrigger canoe with one stickman paddler with dot eyes and a small mouth, open blue ocean, big waves

segments.text: Once they arrived, they were way too heavy to move. So nobody moved them.
shots: S: a stickman with dot eyes and a small mouth in a grass skirt pushing hard against a huge stone disc, straining, sweat drops, palm trees
E: same scene, the stone hasn't moved and the stickman sits down exhausted

segments.text: When a stone changed owners, it stayed exactly where it was. Everyone just remembered who it belonged to.
shots: S: two stickmen with dot eyes and a small mouth in grass skirts, one with a flower necklace, shaking hands in front of a big stone disc in a village clearing

segments.text: And the story goes that one stone sank to the bottom of the sea on the way home.
shots: S: a huge stone disc slipping off a bamboo raft and sinking into stormy dark waves, dramatic, no people visible
S: a giant stone disc resting on the sandy sea floor with fish swimming around it, sunbeams through the water, no people

segments.text: Nobody ever saw it again. But the family that paid for it was still considered rich. Because everyone agreed it was theirs.
shots: S: a stickman with dot eyes and a small mouth in a grass skirt and flower necklace proudly pointing out to sea from a beach, smiling

segments.text: Think about that. Money that nobody can see, that everybody agrees exists.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) staring out at the ocean from a beach with his hand on his chin, thoughtful

segments.text: Remember that idea. Because by the end of this video, you'll realise you use money exactly like that, every single day.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) tapping the side of his head and winking at the viewer, plain warm background

segments.text: Now let's talk about the money you can hold in your hand.
shots: S: close-up of an open palm-shaped wooden dish holding a few shiny ancient gold coins, dark velvet background, no people

segments.text: Around six hundred B.C., in a kingdom called Lydia, in what's now Turkey, someone had a brilliant idea.
shots: S: a stickman king with dot eyes and a small mouth with a golden crown and purple robe on a throne, a glowing lightbulb above his head, ancient palace with columns

segments.text: Take lumps of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver, and stamp them with a lion's head.
shots: S: a stickman metalworker with dot eyes and a small mouth in a leather apron hammering a stamp onto a small golden lump on an anvil, sparks, forge glow
S: close-up of a small lumpy gold coin stamped with a roaring lion's head on a dark cloth, no people

segments.text: That stamp was like a promise from the king. This lump is the real deal. No weighing needed.
shots: S: a stickman shopkeeper with dot eyes and a small mouth in a striped tunic happily accepting a small gold coin and tossing his balance scale aside, market stall

segments.text: Imagine how much faster shopping got. No scales. No arguing. Just hand over a coin.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) in an ancient tunic flipping a gold coin to a fruit seller and catching a pear in return, ancient market

segments.text: These were some of the first coins in history.
shots: S: a few small ancient gold and silver coins glowing on a museum display stand, dark background, spotlight, no people

segments.text: A later king of Lydia, Croesus, went further. He made coins of pure gold and pure silver.
shots: S: a stickman king with dot eyes and a small mouth with a big golden crown holding up a shiny gold coin in one hand and a silver coin in the other, treasure room

segments.text: He became so famous for his wealth that, two and a half thousand years later, people still say 'rich as Croesus'.
shots: S: the stickman king with dot eyes and a small mouth with a big golden crown sitting on a mountain of gold coins, laughing and throwing coins in the air like confetti

segments.text: Coins spread fast. To Greece. To Persia. To Rome.
shots: S: an old parchment map of the ancient Mediterranean with glowing gold coins hopping from Turkey to Greece to Italy along dotted lines, no people

segments.text: And rulers loved them, because they could put their own faces on them. Free advertising, in every pocket.
shots: S: a stickman emperor with dot eyes and a small mouth in a laurel wreath and white toga admiring a coin with a stickman head on it, Roman forum behind
E: same scene, the emperor kisses the coin proudly

segments.text: But coins came with a temptation.
shots: S: the stickman emperor with dot eyes and a small mouth in a laurel wreath rubbing his hands together with a sneaky grin, dark palace room

segments.text: If you're an emperor and you need more money, why not just put less silver in each coin?
shots: S: the stickman emperor with dot eyes and a small mouth in a laurel wreath secretly pouring cheap grey metal into a coin mould instead of shiny silver, workshop

segments.text: That's exactly what Rome did. Over a couple of hundred years, the silver in Roman coins fell from almost pure, to just a few percent.
shots: S: a row of Roman coins from left to right going from shiny bright silver to dull dark grey, plain warm background, no people

segments.text: People noticed. Prices soared. And trust in Roman money crumbled.
shots: S: an angry stickman shopper with dot eyes and a small mouth in a toga holding up a dull grey coin at a Roman bread stall, the baker stickman with dot eyes and a small mouth in an apron shaking his head

segments.text: Remember that word. Trust. It's the secret ingredient of all money.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) holding up a small glowing golden heart in both hands, looking seriously at the viewer, plain warm background

segments.text: There's another problem with coins. They're heavy.
shots: S: a stickman merchant with dot eyes and a small mouth in a blue Chinese robe bent over carrying a huge sack of coins on his back up a mountain road

segments.text: In Sichuan, in China, people used iron coins worth so little that a big purchase meant hauling a whole cart of them.
shots: S: a stickman merchant with dot eyes and a small mouth in a blue Chinese robe pushing a wooden cart overloaded with strings of round iron coins with square holes, old Chinese street, a few tiny distant figures

segments.text: So merchants came up with a clever trick. Leave your heavy coins with a trusted shop, and carry a paper receipt instead.
shots: S: the stickman merchant with dot eyes and a small mouth in a blue robe handing a heavy chest of coins over a counter to a stickman shopkeeper with dot eyes and a small mouth in a red robe, old Chinese shop
E: same scene, the shopkeeper hands back a single sheet of paper and the merchant smiles with relief

segments.text: In ten twenty-four, the Song government took over, and printed the world's first official paper money. The jiaozi.
shots: S: a stickman official with dot eyes and a small mouth in a red Song dynasty robe and black winged hat holding up a large printed paper banknote, wooden printing blocks on a table
S: close-up of an old printed paper banknote with simple patterns and a red seal stamp, no readable text, on a wooden table, no people

segments.text: When the traveller Marco Polo saw paper money in China a couple of centuries later, he could hardly believe it. Paper, worth as much as gold.
shots: S: a stickman traveller with dot eyes and a small mouth in a medieval European cap and cloak staring in amazement at a paper banknote in his hands, Chinese palace courtyard

segments.text: But printing money is even more tempting than shaving coins.
shots: S: a stickman official with dot eyes and a small mouth in a red robe staring at a wooden printing press with a greedy grin, dark workshop

segments.text: Need money? Just print more!
shots: E: same scene, the official cranks the printing press wildly and piles of paper notes fly everywhere

segments.text: Print too much, and every note buys less and less. That's called inflation, and China learned that lesson the hard way, more than once.
shots: S: a stickman shopper with dot eyes and a small mouth in a blue robe holding a huge stack of paper notes to buy one tiny steamed bun at a food stall, shocked face

segments.text: Europe was much slower. And Sweden tried something... interesting.
shots: S: a snowy 1600s Swedish town with red wooden houses and a church, a copper mine entrance on a hill, no people close up

segments.text: In the sixteen hundreds, Sweden had lots of copper. So it made copper money. Giant copper money.
shots: S: a stickman miner with dot eyes and a small mouth in a fur hat holding up a huge flat square copper plate with stamps in each corner, mine entrance behind

segments.text: The biggest was a copper plate weighing almost twenty kilograms. Imagine paying for your groceries with that.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) staggering through a market carrying a huge square copper plate on his back, sweating, fruit stall nearby

segments.text: No surprise, people preferred paper. In sixteen sixty-one, a Swedish bank printed Europe's first banknotes.
shots: S: a stickman banker with dot eyes and a small mouth in a black 1600s coat and white collar proudly holding up a paper banknote, wood-panelled bank office, snowy window

segments.text: For centuries after that, a banknote was a promise. Take it to the bank, and you could swap it for real gold or silver.
shots: S: a stickman customer with dot eyes and a small mouth in a brown coat handing a paper note across a bank counter to a stickman clerk with dot eyes and a small mouth in a black vest who slides back a gold coin

segments.text: That's called the gold standard.
shots: S: a bank vault full of neatly stacked shiny gold bars, a heavy round vault door open, dramatic light, no people

segments.text: Then, in nineteen seventy-one, the United States ended the link between the dollar and gold.
shots: S: a stickman president with dot eyes and a small mouth in a dark suit at a desk speaking into old microphones, a flag behind him, 1970s office
S: big scissors snipping a golden chain that connects a dollar bill to a gold bar, plain background, no people

segments.text: Since then, the money in your pocket isn't backed by gold. It's backed by one thing. Trust.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) pulling a banknote out of his pocket and looking at it, a glowing heart-shaped light around it, plain warm background

segments.text: And when trust breaks, things get crazy.
shots: S: a pile of banknotes catching fire on a dark background, dramatic, no people

segments.text: In Germany in nineteen twenty-three, prices rose so fast that workers were paid twice a day, and rushed to spend their wages before they lost value.
shots: S: a stickman worker with dot eyes and a small mouth in a 1920s flat cap pushing a wheelbarrow full of paper money down a cobbled street, worried face
E: same scene, the worker running fast with the wheelbarrow, papers flying

segments.text: In two thousand nine, Zimbabwe printed a one hundred trillion dollar note. Within weeks, it was almost worthless.
shots: S: close-up of a giant banknote with a long row of zeros and no other readable text, on a table, no people
S: a stickman with dot eyes and a small mouth in a yellow shirt holding a huge stack of banknotes and getting just one egg in return at a shop counter, baffled face

segments.text: And when people have no official money at all, they simply invent their own.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) shrugging with a grin, surrounded by floating shells, a stone disc, a coin and a fish, plain warm background

segments.text: In some American prisons, where cash isn't allowed, inmates have used packets of mackerel as money.
shots: S: a neat stack of small sealed foil fish packets on a metal table, plain grey background, no people

segments.text: Fish. Shells. Stones. Paper. Money is anything enough people agree it is.
shots: S: a row of a fish packet, a cowrie shell, a small stone disc and a paper banknote lined up on a wooden table, soft spotlight, no people

segments.text: Now let's fast forward to you.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) flying out of a swirling time portal into a modern city street, landing on his feet

segments.text: In nineteen fifty, a card called Diners Club let people eat now and pay later. It's often called the first modern credit card.
shots: S: a stickman businessman with dot eyes and a small mouth in a 1950s grey suit and hat proudly showing a small paper card to a stickman waiter with dot eyes and a small mouth in a bow tie, fancy 1950s restaurant

segments.text: Then came cash machines, online banking, and tapping your phone.
shots: S: a stickman with dot eyes and a small mouth in a 1970s orange jacket taking cash from an old cash machine in a brick wall
B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) tapping his smartphone on a payment terminal in a coffee shop, big green tick on the screen

segments.text: So here's a question. How much of all the money out there do you think is actual cash? Half? A quarter?
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) pointing at the viewer with a quiz-show grin, a big question mark floating beside him, plain warm background

segments.text: In the UK, notes and coins are only about three percent of all money.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) staring at a giant pie chart where only a tiny slice is coloured gold, jaw dropped, plain warm background

segments.text: The rest? Just numbers, sitting in bank computers.
shots: S: glowing rows of green numbers flowing between big server racks in a dark data centre, no people

segments.text: Remember the stone at the bottom of the sea? Money nobody can see, that everybody agrees exists?
shots: S: a giant stone disc on the sea floor, glowing digital numbers swirling around it, sunbeams, no people

segments.text: That's your bank balance.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) looking at his phone screen with a shocked, amazed face, a glowing number above the phone, city street

segments.text: And some people wondered: what if money didn't need banks at all?
shots: S: a stickman with dot eyes and a small mouth in a dark hoodie typing on a laptop in a dark room, face lit by the screen

segments.text: In two thousand nine, someone using the name Satoshi Nakamoto launched Bitcoin. Digital money, with no bank in charge.
shots: S: the stickman with dot eyes and a small mouth in a dark hoodie leaning back from the laptop as a big glowing golden coin with a B symbol floats above the screen, dark room

segments.text: A year later, a programmer in Florida paid ten thousand bitcoins for two pizzas.
shots: S: a stickman programmer with dot eyes and a small mouth in glasses and a t-shirt happily holding two pizza boxes at his front door, sunny Florida house with a palm tree

segments.text: Years later, those coins were worth hundreds of millions of dollars. Probably the most expensive pizzas in history.
shots: E: same scene, the programmer's eyes go wide as glowing golden coins fly out of the pizza boxes

segments.text: So, back to that burger joint.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) at the diner counter clutching his teal hoodie, the giant burger still in front of him, nervous face

segments.text: Your card got declined. The cook wants your hoodie.
shots: S: the stickman cook with dot eyes and a small mouth in a white chef hat holding out his hand expectantly across the diner counter, raised eyebrow

segments.text: You open your banking app, and realise you just forgot to move money onto your card.
shots: B: close-up of Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) looking at his phone screen and facepalming, diner background
E: same scene, Byte grinning sheepishly at the viewer

segments.text: Tap. Beep. Paid. In less than a second.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) tapping his phone on the diner card reader which shows a big green tick, triumphant face

segments.text: No goat. No shells. No four-tonne stone. Just a number moving from one computer to another.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) biting into the giant burger, blissful face, diner counter

segments.text: Five thousand years of clay, shells, stones, gold and paper... all so you could buy a burger with a number on a screen.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) leaning back on his diner stool with an empty plate, floating icons of a clay tablet, a shell, a stone disc, a gold coin and a banknote around him, satisfied

segments.text: And it works for one simple reason. Everyone agrees it does.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) giving the viewer a confident thumbs up with a smile, diner background

segments.text: So, what should we explore next? Tell us in the comments. And subscribe to ByteSized AI, so you don't miss the next one.
shots: B: Byte (the only stickman in an orange cap and teal hoodie) waving goodbye at the viewer outside the diner at sunset, a neon burger sign with no words

meta.hook_line: Imagine your card gets declined and the cook wants your hoodie instead. For most of history, that's how it worked. So how did we end up paying with invisible numbers?
meta.summary: From the barter myth to Bitcoin: clay receipts and debt cancellations in Mesopotamia, cowrie shells, the four-tonne stone money of Yap, Lydia's lion coins and 'rich as Croesus', Rome's shrinking silver, China's paper money, Sweden's 20 kg copper plates, the gold standard, hyperinflation, prison mackerel, and why only about 3% of money is cash.
bullets: Why barter probably never worked the way school books say

Cowrie shells and the giant stone money of Yap
Lydia's lion coins, Croesus, and how Rome ruined its silver

Sweden's copper plates, the gold standard and 1971
Hyperinflation, prison mackerel, credit cards and Bitcoin pizza
